newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Rural exodus not always reversible - EU's Fischler.
newsitem.headline: Rural exodus not always reversible - EU's Fischler.

text.p: The exodus from some country areas to cities which are heading for social crisis cannot be reversed, EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said on Thursday.

In a speech to a three-day agriculture and rural development conference in Cork, Ireland, Fischler argued for an integrated and simplified administrative approach to rural areas of the European Union.
The speech was released in Brussels.

Spelling out for the first time the view that the EU's support for agriculture has been too narrowly focused, he said: "I think we are still concentrating unduly on the maintainance and continued development of the sectoral aspects of rural areas.
"Too little emphasis is still being placed on the strong inter-relationships with other policies and the need for diversification," he added.

Outlining the challenges facing the EU, he said time was running out and rural Europe faced constantly growing dangers. Modern infrastructures were growing at "a dizzy speed" and "we are perhaps too late already".
"In some regions the rural exodus can no longer be reversed," he told the conference.

He said structural weaknesses were destroying the prospects of rural areas which were dwindling away because of gaps in their infrastructure, listing problems of too few jobs, inadequate services and not enough opportunities for basic or further training.
His comments were seen as a clear warning to farmers that they can expect dramatic changes in the way EU funds are applied in the future.

"The situation on the labour market is further exacerbated by serious difficulties in the agricultural sector, where constantly rising productivity and increasing pressure of competition are also drastically reducing the number of jobs available...," Fischler said
In future the role of the Commission would be to foster the creation of jobs outside agriculture and improve the rural infrastructure, he said.
He highlighted public sensitivity to what he called "the negative environmental effects of farming" and said society was interested in paying farmers for their services to the environment.
